# Where we have been

## The whole course in one slide {.smaller}

- **Deterministic models**: write the likelihood, sample it with MCMC
- **Diagnostics**: did the sampler work? R̂, ESS, divergences
- **Model checking**: is the model any good? Prior and posterior predictive checks
- **Stochastic models**: the likelihood becomes an integral over trajectories
- **Particle filters**: estimate that integral by simulation
- **pMCMC**: sample with an estimated likelihood, and it still targets the right posterior
- **Observation models**: a likelihood is a distance function you committed to
- **ABC**: choose the distance instead, and drop the likelihood entirely

::: {.fragment}
The question you actually go home with: [which of these does *my* problem
need?]{.alert}
:::

# Two questions decide it

## Question one

::: {.r-fit-text}
Can you write down and evaluate
$$p(\text{data} \mid \theta)?$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Yes** — everything from grid search to NUTS is open to you
- **No** — simulation-based territory: particle filters, pMCMC, ABC
:::

## Question two

::: {.r-fit-text}
Can you [differentiate]{.alert} it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- **Yes** — use NUTS. It is the default for a reason
- **No** — adaptive Metropolis-Hastings, RAM, or a simulation-based method
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is the question people forget to ask before picking a tool.
:::

## The map {.smaller}

| Method | Needs | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Grid search | likelihood | hopeless past 2-3 parameters |
| Metropolis-Hastings | likelihood | cheap steps, many of them |
| RAM / adaptive MH | likelihood | as MH, tunes itself |
| **NUTS** | likelihood **and gradient** | expensive steps, few of them |
| Particle filter + PMMH | stochastic simulator | very expensive |
| ABC | simulator only | expensive and approximate |

::: {.fragment}
Down the table needs **less** of you, so it works on harder models. Generality is
never free.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Variational inference** sits outside this ordering: it needs everything NUTS
needs, and trades accuracy for speed rather than assumptions for cost.
:::

## Do not pay for generality you do not need

::: {.fragment}
Fitting a deterministic model with ABC is not *wrong*.
:::

::: {.fragment}
It is thousands of times slower than NUTS, and less accurate.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Take the most [specific]{.alert} method your problem allows.
:::

# What actually goes wrong

## It is almost never the sampler {.smaller}

::: {.fragment}
**The observation model** — Poisson on overdispersed data: overconfident
posterior, one bad day dominates the fit.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The priors** — `Uniform(1, 20)` on $R_0$ says 19 is as plausible as 2.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Identifiability** — if two parameters trade off, the data cannot separate them
and no sampler will. This is a property of model and data, not of the algorithm.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The model** — one that cannot produce your data will not be rescued by better
inference.
:::

## Two things this map leaves out {.smaller}

**States, not just parameters.** The posterior factorises as
$$p(x, \theta \mid y) = p(\theta \mid y)\, p(x \mid \theta, y)$$
Parameter fitting is the first factor. A particle filter also gives you the
second: what the epidemic was actually doing.

::: {.fragment}
**Comparing models, not just fitting one.** SEITL against SEIT4L was a question no
amount of sampling one model answers. Fit both, then compare — predictive
performance, or the marginal likelihood if you can get at it.
:::

## The asymmetry worth remembering

Sampler problems are [loud]{.alert}: R̂, divergences, ugly trace plots.

::: {.fragment}
Model problems are [silent]{.alert}. A converged chain from a bad model looks
exactly like a converged chain from a good one.
:::

::: {.fragment}
That is why model checking is a separate job from diagnostics.
:::

# Where you go next

## Two directions {.smaller}

**Scale** — many models, or one model across many regions.

```julia
sample(model, NUTS(), MCMCThreads(), 1000, 4)
```

That is the whole change needed to run four chains in parallel.

::: {.fragment}
**Structure** — real data arrives late, incomplete, and from several streams at
once. Reporting delays, nowcasting, evidence synthesis.

The model gets more elaborate. The inference machinery stays the same.
:::

## {{< fa laptop-code >}} Your Turn {background-color="#447099" transition="fade-in"}

Take a model you actually want to fit.

- Can you write down the likelihood? If not, what stops you?
- Can you differentiate it?
- Which row of the table does that leave you on?
- What would you check first if the answer looked wrong?

The last one usually changes people's plans.
